title: the most misunderstood room in the building
hookLine: the booth, the nerves, and why a person and not just a prayer
carry: say it out loud, then it's smaller

cards: Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. Plenty of people raised Catholic can still say the opening line, and still remember the nerves: the line outside the booth, the list rehearsed in your head, the little screen.
Movies made it a courtroom, or a punch line. And later comes the fair question: why tell a person? Why not just tell God?

teach.b: Catholics call it the sacrament of reconciliation; most just say confession. The answer to why a person starts on Easter night.
In John's Gospel, the risen Jesus breathes on his friends and says, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them."
Catholics believe that from then on, forgiveness was meant to be spoken out loud, through a person, and heard out loud too.
God does the forgiving; the priest speaks for him, and for the Church, since a wrong never touches just one person. What happens is simple.

teach.h: BEHIND A SCREEN OR FACE TO FACE.
teach.b: You can kneel behind a screen or sit face to face. You say what you've done, plainly, in your own words.

The priest listens, gives a penance, usually a prayer or a small act to make things right, and then says the words of absolution: you're forgiven, in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.
One rule is absolute: the seal. A priest may never reveal what he hears, to anyone, for any reason. And if it's been years, and that's the very thing keeping you away, here's what's true.

Mass is open to you; you can go and simply not receive communion until you're ready. You can start with: it's been a long time, and I don't remember how. Priests hear it often, and helping you through is part of the job.

Nervous is normal. Some people write their list on a scrap of paper, bring it in, and tear it up afterward. Catholics believe the forgiveness is real even if you walk out feeling awkward, or nothing at all.
Something huge in the dark at two in the morning gets edges once it's spoken.

how: Catholics go to confession with a priest, anonymously behind a screen or face to face, name their sins, receive a small penance, and hear the words of absolution; many go before Christmas and Easter, and some go monthly.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, think of one thing you've been carrying and never said out loud. On the second, name it to yourself in one plain sentence.
On the third, breathe out, and notice whether it feels any different now that it has a name.

wordCard.voice: Confession. Saying it out loud, and hearing out loud that you're forgiven. Third word.

orig.note: Latin: I confess. the first word of the prayer of confession said at the start of Mass.

carryVoice: Your line: say it out loud, then it's smaller. That's the whole secret of the little room. Day three.
